per_question.question: How does NASA define 'systems engineering'?
per_question.generated_answer:
NASA defines "systems engineering" as a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system [1], [3].

Additional context clarifies that a "system" is the combination of elements—hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes, and procedures—that function together to produce the capability required to meet a need, with system-level results including qualities, properties, characteristics, functions, behavior, and performance. The value added by the system as a whole, beyond what its individual parts contribute independently, comes primarily from the relationships among the parts (i.e., how they are interconnected) [1].

Systems engineering is further described as "a way of looking at the 'big picture' when making technical decisions," and as a methodology for achieving stakeholder functional, physical, and operational performance requirements within cost, schedule, and other constraints over the planned life of the system—essentially, "a logical way of thinking" [1].

It is also characterized as "the art and science of developing an operable system capable of meeting requirements within often opposed constraints," and as a holistic, integrative discipline that balances the contributions of many engineering disciplines (structural, electrical, mechanical, power, human factors, etc.) to produce a coherent whole not dominated by any single discipline's perspective. It seeks a safe and balanced design amid conflicting constraints [1].

per_question.question: Per NPR 7123.1, what is the difference between applying an SE process 'iteratively' versus 'recursively'?
per_question.generated_answer:
Per NPR 7123.1, the distinction is as follows:

- **Iterative**: The "application of a process to the same product or set of products to correct a discovered discrepancy or other variation from requirements" [2], [5].

- **Recursive**: Defined as adding value to the system "by the repeated application of processes to design next lower layer system products or to realize next upper layer end products within the system structure. This also applies to repeating application of the same processes to the system structure in the next life cycle phase to mature the system definition and satisfy phase success criteria" [1], [2], [5].

In short, iteration involves reapplying a process to the *same* product to fix errors or discrepancies, while recursion involves reapplying the *same* processes to *different* layers of the system structure (moving up or down the product hierarchy) or across life cycle phases to mature the system definition [1], [2], [5].
